title: Seleucid Iran
subtitle: 330–148 BC · Alexander's Successors and the Loss of the Upper Satrapies

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Seleucid Kings, the Upper Satrapies command, and the Frataraka of Persis

entries.label: Seleucus I — the satrap who won the East
entries.hint: Seleucus secured Babylon in 312 BC — the year later reckoned the start of the Seleucid Era — then extended his authority east through Media and Persis to the Indus, before ceding the Indian satrapies to Chandragupta Maurya in exchange for 500 war elephants and a marriage alliance around 303 BC.
entries.note: Appian, Syriaca 55; Strabo, Geography 15.2.9 (the elephant treaty).

entries.label: Antiochus I — holding the Upper Satrapies
entries.hint: Antiochus I had governed the eastern satrapies as his father's co-ruler for over a decade before succeeding alone in 281 BC — deep personal familiarity with Iran and Bactria that shaped his reign's emphasis on garrisoning and refounding cities across the plateau rather than campaigning further east.
entries.note: Appian, Syriaca 62; Memnon of Heraclea, History of Heraclea (via Photius), on the co-rule arrangement.

entries.label: Antiochus II and Seleucus II — Bactria and Parthia break away
entries.hint: During these two reigns the empire's grip on its farthest satrapies failed: the Bactrian satrap Diodotus declared independence around 250 BC, and the Parni chieftain Arsaces seized Parthia from the rebel satrap Andragoras around 247 BC — the two founding secessions that define this folio's central story.
entries.note: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 41.4; Strabo, Geography 11.9.2–3.

entries.label: Antiochus III the Great — the Anabasis and the reconquest of the East
entries.hint: Antiochus III's great eastern campaign of 212–205 BC marched through Media, besieged Bactra for two years, and forced both the Parthian king Arsaces II and the Bactrian king Euthydemus I to accept nominal vassalage — the last moment Seleucid authority was substantively restored over Iran, before his defeat by Rome at Magnesia in 190 BC redirected the empire's attention permanently westward.
entries.note: Polybius, Histories 10.28–31, 10.49, 11.34 (the Anabasis); Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 37.37–44 (Magnesia).

entries.label: The Last Seleucids and the Loss of Iran
entries.hint: Seleucus IV and Antiochus IV directed the kingdom's shrinking resources toward Judea and Egypt rather than the East. In 148 BC the Parthian king Mithridates I conquered Media outright, and Persis soon followed — ending Seleucid rule in Iran for good, a generation before the dynasty itself finally collapsed in Syria.
entries.note: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 41.6; Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 33.18 (Mithridates I in Media).

entries.label: The Strategos of the Upper Satrapies
entries.hint: Antiochus III formalised a supra-provincial military command, the 'strategos of the Upper Satrapies,' headquartered at Ecbatana and overseeing Media, Persis, Parthia and the eastern frontier as a single defensive command — recognition that the East needed unified rather than piecemeal administration, though the office could not ultimately reverse the territorial losses.
entries.note: Polybius, Histories 5.40–54 (the office under Molon's revolt); Getzel Cohen, The Hellenistic Settlements in the East (2013).

entries.label: The Greek Cities of the Iranian Plateau
entries.hint: Seleucid kings refounded or established Greek poleis across Media and Persis — Europos at Rhagae, Antioch-in-Persis among them — bringing the civic institutions of the gymnasium and the theatre to the Iranian plateau, settled by veteran-colonists alongside the existing Iranian population.
entries.note: Strabo, Geography 11.13.6 (Rhagae/Europos); Pliny the Elder, Natural History 6.135 (Antioch-in-Persis).

entries.label: The Frataraka — Persis under Seleucid Suzerainty
entries.hint: Appointed originally as Seleucid provincial governors and high priests of the Persepolis temple, the frataraka ('forerunners') of Persis progressively acted as autonomous local rulers, striking their own coinage stamped with fire-altars and titulature deliberately echoing Achaemenid kingship — the clearest continuous thread of Persian identity running beneath Greek imperial rule.
entries.note: Frataraka coin series, British Museum and Cabinet des Médailles; Josef Wiesehöfer, 'Frataraka Rule in Seleucid Persis' (2011).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Wars of the Successors and the secession of Parthia and Bactria

entries.label: Seleucus's Eastern Campaign
entries.hint: Seleucus recovered Babylon in 312 BC against Antigonus's forces, then campaigned east through Media, Persis and Bactria to the Indus valley, before Chandragupta Maurya's army checked his advance and the two agreed a treaty ceding the Indian territories in exchange for elephants and peace.
entries.note: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 19.90–92; Strabo, Geography 15.2.9.

entries.group: The Secession of Parthia and Bactria
entries.label: The Secession of Bactria
entries.hint: The Seleucid satrap of Bactria, Diodotus, declared himself an independent king rather than defer to the distant court — Justin describes Parthia's own revolt as breaking out 'at almost the same time,' the opening move in the collapse of Seleucid authority across the Upper Satrapies.
entries.note: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 41.4; Strabo, Geography 11.9.3.

entries.group: The Secession of Parthia and Bactria
entries.label: Arsaces and the Parthian Conquest of Parthia
entries.hint: The Parni chieftain Arsaces invaded the Parthian satrapy and killed the rebel Seleucid satrap Andragoras, founding the dynasty that would eventually take his name — the Arsacid state that, two centuries later, would inherit the whole of Iran from the Seleucids piece by piece.
entries.note: Strabo, Geography 11.9.2–3; Arsacid dynastic tradition recorded in Justin, Epitome 41.4–5.

entries.label: The Siege of Bactra and the Eastern Anabasis
entries.hint: Antiochus III marched through Media into Parthia, forced Arsaces II to submit, then besieged Euthydemus I of Bactria in Bactra for two years before agreeing terms recognising Bactrian kingship as a vassal state — a treaty sealed, Polybius reports, by the marriage of a Seleucid princess to Euthydemus's son Demetrius.
entries.note: Polybius, Histories 10.49, 11.34.

entries.label: The Battle of Magnesia
entries.hint: Fought far from Iran, Antiochus III's catastrophic defeat by Rome at Magnesia and the crushing indemnity of the Peace of Apamea (188 BC) that followed permanently redirected Seleucid resources and attention westward, leaving the Upper Satrapies without the sustained royal presence that had briefly reclaimed them.
entries.note: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 37.37–44; Polybius, Histories 21.42 (the Peace of Apamea terms).

entries.label: Mithridates I's Conquest of Media
entries.hint: The Parthian king Mithridates I invaded and conquered Media, ending Seleucid rule over the Iranian plateau's core province; Persis and the remaining Upper Satrapies fell away in the years immediately following, closing the Seleucid chapter of Iran's history for good.
entries.note: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 33.18; Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 41.6.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Colonization policy, military land grants, and the fiscal integration of the East

entries.label: Seleucus's Refoundation Policy
entries.hint: Seleucus I and his immediate successors systematically renamed and refounded existing cities across Media and Persis as Greek-style poleis — Ecbatana itself briefly styled 'Epiphaneia' — layering a Greek civic and administrative structure over the existing Iranian urban fabric rather than replacing it outright.
entries.note: Appian, Syriaca 57 (Seleucus's city foundations generally); Getzel Cohen, The Hellenistic Settlements in the East (2013).

entries.label: The Royal Land Grant System
entries.hint: Following Achaemenid precedent, Seleucid kings granted royal land (basilike ge) to Greek and Macedonian military settlers (katoikoi) across Media and Persis in exchange for hereditary military service — the institutional backbone of the colonist population documented in the new poleis.
entries.note: Getzel Cohen, The Hellenistic Settlements in the East (2013); comparanda from the Seleucid land-grant inscriptions of Asia Minor (e.g. the Aristodicides dossier).

entries.label: Antiochus I's Model of Temple Patronage
entries.hint: Antiochus I's foundation cylinder from Borsippa, recording his restoration of the Ezida temple in the traditional style of a Babylonian king, exemplifies the empire-wide Seleucid policy of patronising local cults in their own idiom — the same approach extended to the Persepolis temple establishment the frataraka of Persis administered.
entries.note: Antiochus I Cylinder (British Museum BM 36277).
keywords: Antiochus I Model of Temple Patronage

entries.label: The Upper Satrapies in the Royal Economy
entries.hint: Media and Persis continued to render tribute and troop levies to the Seleucid crown on essentially the Achaemenid model, integrated into an empire-wide fiscal system centred on the western capitals — a continuity that made the East's eventual secession a direct loss to the royal treasury, not merely a symbolic one.
entries.note: Polybius, Histories 5.40–54 (Molon's revolt exploiting the East's fiscal and military weight).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Hellenistic ruler cult, Zoroastrian continuity, and the religion of the colonists

entries.label: The Later Memory of 'Alexander's' Religious Damage
entries.hint: Centuries later, Zoroastrian priestly tradition — the Sasanian-era Kartir inscriptions and the Denkard — blamed 'the accursed Alexander' for burning the Avesta and scattering the priesthood, a retrospective judgment on this whole Hellenistic period that does not match the archaeological record of continued fire-temple use, but reveals how later Zoroastrians came to remember Greek rule.
entries.note: Denkard, Book 4 (on the Avesta's Hellenistic-era dispersal, as later remembered); Kartir's inscriptions (e.g. Naqsh-e Rajab), 3rd century AD.

entries.label: Greek Cults among the Colonists
entries.hint: Greek and Macedonian settlers in the new poleis of Media and Persis maintained their own cults of Zeus, Apollo and the deified Seleucid founders, organised around the gymnasium and civic festival calendar familiar from Hellenistic cities everywhere else, alongside — rather than replacing — existing Iranian religious life.
entries.note: Comparative epigraphic evidence from Hellenistic gymnasium inscriptions across the Seleucid East; Rachel Mairs, The Hellenistic Far East (2014).

entries.label: The Nihavand Inscription — the Cult of Queen Laodice
entries.hint: A decree of Antiochus III found at Nihavand in Media orders the establishment of worship for his wife Queen Laodice in temples throughout the kingdom — direct epigraphic proof that Hellenistic ruler-cult institutions reached deep into the Iranian plateau, not only the Mediterranean core of the empire.
entries.note: Nihavand inscription of Antiochus III (SEG 37.1010).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Greek civic art on the Iranian plateau, and the fire-altar coinage of Persis

entries.label: The Greek Civic Plan at Rhagae
entries.hint: Europos at Rhagae was laid out with the gridded street plan, gymnasium and theatre standard to a Hellenistic polis — Greek civic architecture transplanted onto a Median site with an urban history stretching back centuries before Alexander.
entries.note: Strabo, Geography 11.13.6; comparative Hellenistic urban planning, Getzel Cohen (2013).

entries.label: The Fire-Altar Coinage of the Frataraka
entries.hint: Frataraka coins struck at Persepolis pair Greek minting technique and weight standards with distinctly Iranian imagery — a standing archer-king before a fire-altar — a deliberate visual fusion asserting continuity with Achaemenid kingship on coinage that still circulated under nominal Seleucid authority.
entries.note: Frataraka coin series, British Museum and Cabinet des Médailles.

entries.label: Gymnasium Musical Contests in the New Poleis
entries.hint: Hellenistic gymnasium inscriptions from across the Seleucid East record musical and choral contests as a standard part of civic festival life, funded by a gymnasiarch — the same institutional pattern very likely operated in the new poleis of Media and Persis, though no inscription naming individual performers survives there directly.
entries.note: Comparative Seleucid-era gymnasium inscriptions (e.g. from Ai-Khanoum and Failaka); Rachel Mairs, The Hellenistic Far East (2014).

entries.label: The Herakles of Behistun
entries.hint: A reclining stone statue of Herakles carved into the base of Mount Behistun — the same cliff Darius I had used three centuries earlier — carries a Greek dedicatory inscription naming the Seleucid official Hyacinthus, precisely dated to 148 BC, the very year Seleucid rule in Media finally ended.
entries.note: Herakles of Behistun statue and inscription, in situ, Kermanshah Province; Louis Robert, 'Le relief et l'inscription d'Héraclès à Bisotun' (1963).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Geography, historiography, and the memory of Achaemenid kingship

entries.label: Berossus's Babyloniaca, Dedicated to Antiochus I
entries.hint: The Babylonian priest Berossus composed a Greek-language history of Mesopotamia and the wider East dedicated to Antiochus I — part of a broader Seleucid-era pattern of local priestly elites translating their own traditions into the empire's Greek administrative language for a royal audience.
entries.note: Berossus, Babyloniaca (surviving only in later excerpts via Josephus, Eusebius and Syncellus).

entries.label: Patrocles's Survey of the Caspian
entries.hint: Commissioned by Seleucus I and Antiochus I, the admiral Patrocles surveyed the Caspian Sea and concluded — mistakenly, but influentially — that it connected to a northern ocean, geographic knowledge that fed directly into how Eratosthenes and later Greek geographers mapped the whole of Asia.
entries.note: Strabo, Geography 2.1.17, 11.6.1 (citing Patrocles directly).

entries.label: The Memory of Cyrus in Seleucid Ideology
entries.hint: Polybius's account of Antiochus III's eastern Anabasis frames the king explicitly against the memory of Cyrus the Great's conquests over the same ground — evidence that Seleucid kings actively invoked Achaemenid universal-kingship rhetoric to legitimate their rule over Iran, rather than presenting themselves purely as Greek conquerors.
entries.note: Polybius, Histories 10.27–31 (the eastern campaign narrated with explicit Achaemenid comparison).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Trade, minting, and the agrarian base of the military colonies

entries.label: The Royal Road in the Hellenistic Trade World
entries.hint: The old Achaemenid road network continued to carry Mediterranean and Indian goods across Media and Persis under Seleucid administration, now feeding into a much larger Hellenistic trade world stretching from the Aegean to the Indus, itself connected by Seleucus's own treaty with Chandragupta Maurya.
entries.note: Strabo, Geography 15.1.4 (the India route); Getzel Cohen, The Hellenistic Settlements in the East (2013).

entries.label: The Ecbatana Mint
entries.hint: Ecbatana operated as one of the Seleucid empire's major mints, striking silver tetradrachms on the Attic weight standard alongside the western mints — a concrete sign that Media remained financially integrated into the wider Seleucid monetary system until the very end of the kingdom's hold on Iran.
entries.note: Arthur Houghton and Catharine Lorber, Seleucid Coins: A Comprehensive Catalogue (2002).

entries.label: Military Colonist Estates on the Plateau
entries.hint: The qanat-fed agricultural estates granted to Greek and Macedonian military colonists under the royal land-grant system generated the surplus that supported both the settlers' hereditary military obligation and the crown's own revenues — continuity of Achaemenid-era irrigation infrastructure repurposed for a new landholding class.
entries.note: Getzel Cohen, The Hellenistic Settlements in the East (2013); qanat survey evidence, Fars and Media provinces.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Roads, siege engineering, and the qanats under new administration

entries.label: Maintaining the Royal Road
entries.hint: Seleucid administration maintained and garrisoned the Achaemenid Royal Road's staging posts across Media and Persis, preserving the empire's fastest communication and troop-movement corridor even as direct royal authority over its eastern end steadily weakened.
entries.note: Herodotus's original description (Histories 5.52–53) remained the template; Seleucid-era milestone and garrison evidence, Getzel Cohen (2013).

entries.label: Qanat Engineering under New Administration
entries.hint: The underground qanat channels that had underwritten Achaemenid agriculture continued in use and extension under Seleucid and frataraka administration alike — infrastructure that outlasted the dynasty that inherited it and the one that displaced it in turn.
entries.note: Polybius, Histories 10.28 (on qanats in Media, describing an established, long-functioning technology).

entries.label: The Siege Works at Bactra
entries.hint: Antiochus III's two-year siege of Bactra deployed the full Hellenistic siege repertoire — circumvallation, siege towers, and blockade — against one of the best-fortified cities of the Iranian and Central Asian world, a technical effort that ultimately produced a negotiated vassal treaty rather than the city's capture.
entries.note: Polybius, Histories 10.49.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Treaties with India and the vassal kingdoms, and the fusion of Greek and Iranian forms

entries.label: The Seleucus–Chandragupta Treaty
entries.hint: Seleucus I ceded the easternmost satrapies to the Mauryan emperor Chandragupta in exchange for 500 war elephants and a marriage alliance, establishing a lasting diplomatic relationship — Seleucid ambassadors, most famously Megasthenes, subsequently resided at the Mauryan court, routed through Iran on the journey east.
entries.note: Strabo, Geography 15.2.9; Appian, Syriaca 55.

entries.label: Greek and Iranian Fusion in Frataraka Coinage
entries.hint: Frataraka coins fusing Greek die-cutting technique with Zoroastrian fire-altar and archer-king imagery are among the clearest material evidence anywhere in the Hellenistic world of a subject culture actively reshaping the conqueror's own technology to assert its own continuity, rather than simply absorbing Greek forms wholesale.
entries.note: Frataraka coin series, British Museum and Cabinet des Médailles; Josef Wiesehöfer, 'Frataraka Rule in Seleucid Persis' (2011).

entries.label: Antiochus III's Vassal Treaties with Parthia and Bactria
entries.hint: Rather than reconquer Parthia and Bactria outright, Antiochus III negotiated formal recognition of Arsaces II and Euthydemus I as vassal kings owing tribute and military support — a diplomatic settlement papering over a military reality the Seleucids could no longer fully reverse.
entries.note: Polybius, Histories 10.49, 11.34.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Diadochi wars and the piecemeal loss of the Upper Satrapies

entries.label: The Wars of the Successors Reshape the East
entries.hint: Alexander's death in 323 BC set off two decades of warfare among his generals; the eastern satrapies — Media, Persis, Bactria — changed hands repeatedly before Seleucus's recovery of Babylon in 312 BC gave the region a stable, if distant, master for the first time since the conquest.
entries.note: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 18–19 (the Wars of the Diadochi).
keywords: Wars of the Successors Reshape the East

entries.label: The Greek and Macedonian Settlement Wave
entries.hint: Tens of thousands of Greek and Macedonian veterans and their families settled across Media and Persis as military colonists over the third century BC, the demographic layer underlying the new poleis and the royal land-grant system — a substantial and lasting population movement into the Iranian plateau from the Mediterranean world.
entries.note: Getzel Cohen, The Hellenistic Settlements in the East (2013); Rachel Mairs, The Hellenistic Far East (2014).

entries.label: The Piecemeal Loss of the Upper Satrapies
entries.hint: Bactria's secession around 250 BC and Parthia's around 247 BC were not single ruptures but the opening of a century-long process — briefly reversed by Antiochus III's Anabasis — by which the Seleucid Empire lost the Iranian plateau one province at a time, ending with Mithridates I's conquest of Media in 148 BC.
entries.note: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 41.4–6; Josef Wiesehöfer, Ancient Persia (2001 English ed.).
keywords: Piecemeal Loss of the Upper Satrapies

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Queenship, colonial status, and the Greek-Iranian elite

entries.label: 'Persians' and 'Hellenes' as Civic Categories
entries.hint: Civic inscriptions from Hellenistic poleis across the Seleucid East distinguish citizen 'Hellenes' from the surrounding 'Persian' or native population in matters of tax status and civic participation — a new administrative and legal category imposed on a population that had, a few generations earlier, been simply Achaemenid subjects with no such formal distinction.
entries.note: Comparative Seleucid-era civic status inscriptions (e.g. from Failaka/Ikaros and Susa); Rachel Mairs, The Hellenistic Far East (2014).

entries.label: Land Lost to the Colonist System
entries.hint: The royal land-grant system that rewarded Greek and Macedonian veterans with hereditary estates necessarily drew on land and labour previously held by the existing Iranian agricultural population — a redistribution the Greek sources, written from the colonists' perspective, rarely describe from the other side.
entries.note: Getzel Cohen, The Hellenistic Settlements in the East (2013), on the land-grant system's demographic base.

entries.label: Queen Laodice's Formal Cult Status
entries.hint: Antiochus III's decree establishing empire-wide worship of Queen Laodice gave a royal woman a formal religious status distinct from — and considerably more institutionalised than — the informal political influence Achaemenid queens like Atossa and Parysatis had wielded three centuries earlier, a genuinely new category of female authority introduced with Hellenistic rule.
entries.note: Nihavand inscription of Antiochus III (SEG 37.1010).
